name: afl++
why: A coverage-guided fuzzer that evolves inputs to break programs, a fascinating way to watch software get taken apart.

brief.what_it_is: AFL++ is a fuzzing framework: a tool that generates many mutated inputs and feeds them to a target program to find crashes and hangs. You compile the target with AFL++'s compiler wrappers (afl-cc, afl-c++), then run afl-fuzz against it with a directory of seed inputs. The fuzzer mutates those inputs and keeps the ones that reach new code paths. Crashes and hangs are written to crashes/ and hangs/ under the output directory, and afl-fuzz shows a status screen while it runs. The package also ships helpers such as afl-cmin and afl-tmin for corpus minimization, afl-showmap for coverage maps, and afl-plot for graphs, plus binary-only instrumentation modes (QEMU, Unicorn, QBDI).
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says AFLplusplus is the daughter of American Fuzzy Lop by Michal 'lcamtuf' Zalewski and was created to merge the best features developed for the AFL family that were never merged into AFL, which the homepage says has not been updated since November 2017. The README calls it 'a superior fork to Google's AFL - more speed, more and better mutations, more and better instrumentation, custom module support, etc.'
brief.how_it_works: Targets are built with instrumentation (LLVM mode, afl-as, or the GCC plugin) so the fuzzer can observe which code paths each input exercises. afl-fuzz then mutates seed inputs and keeps those that discover new coverage. The README also describes a CMPLOG option (AFL_LLVM_CMPLOG=1 with afl-clang-fast), which the README recommends for comparisons; its mechanism was not explained in the pages read.

commands_seen.context: Pulls the prebuilt AFL++ image from Docker Hub (x86_64 and arm64), the README's first suggested route.
Runs the container with your target source mounted at /src.

Quick-start step 3: fuzzes a program that reads from stdin, with seeds in seeds_dir and results in output_dir. The README wraps this across two lines with a backslash; it is joined here.

brief.install_notes: The README recommends building from source and points to docs/INSTALL.md for that; I did not open that file. Quick start: compile the target with afl-cc/afl-c++ (for example via CC= and CXX= at configure time). Dictionaries for verbose formats are described in dictionaries/README.md. Docker is the fastest route; the image is rebuilt on pushes to the stable branch, and aflplusplus/aflplusplus:dev tracks the development branch. The README also says to read the fuzzing risks section in docs/fuzzing_in_depth.md before starting. Homebrew is not mentioned in the pages I read.
brief.standout: The license is split per file: afl-fuzz is AGPL-3.0-or-later, but code compiled into a harness stays Apache-2.0, and each file's SPDX header decides. The README also offers a commercial license that is 'obtained by donating to a good cause' (EUR 20,000 to the EFF or CCC), with the project receiving no money.
brief.status: maintained. The README lists release version 5.03c and GitHub version 5.04a, names four active maintainers, says the dev branch accepts pull requests, and the homepage lists current sponsors. I did not see a last-commit date, so the exact recency is unverified.
brief.caveats: The 'dev' branch is described in the README as 'bleeding edge and you might catch a checkout which does not compile or has a bug'. AGPL-3.0 applies to the combined afl-fuzz binary; commercial use without AGPL compliance requires the EUR 20,000 donation, renewable yearly. The README asks users to read the common-sense fuzzing risks before running it. The brew caveats field is empty. I did not check the build requirements in docs/INSTALL.md.
quotes: AFL++ is a superior fork to Google's AFL - more speed, more and better mutations, more and better instrumentation, custom module support, etc.
Everything compiled into a fuzzing harness is and will stay Apache 2.0 licensed.
We cannot stress this enough - if you want to fuzz effectively, read the docs/fuzzing_in_depth.md document!

judge.reason: AFL++ makes coverage-guided fuzzing tangible: it evolves inputs to explore new code paths and uncover crashes, opening a powerful way to take software apart.

entry.title: AFL++
entry.tldr: A coverage-guided fuzzer that mutates seed inputs, watches which code paths they reach, and keeps the ones that find new ones, until something crashes.
entry.deeper_look:
AFL++ is a fuzzing framework. You compile a target program with its compiler wrappers (`afl-cc`, `afl-c++`) so the binary reports which code paths each input exercises. Then `afl-fuzz` takes a directory of seed inputs, mutates them, and keeps any mutation that reaches new code. Crashes and hangs are saved under `crashes/` and `hangs/` in the output directory, and a status screen updates while it runs.

The idea underneath is that the program itself is the feedback signal. Random bytes rarely get past the first input check. Keeping inputs that reach new coverage lets the fuzzer gradually learn the shape of a file format or protocol without being told. The package also ships helpers: `afl-cmin` and `afl-tmin` shrink a corpus and individual inputs, `afl-showmap` prints coverage maps, and `afl-plot` draws graphs. There are binary-only modes (QEMU, Unicorn, QBDI) for targets you cannot recompile.

AFL++ is a community fork of American Fuzzy Lop by Michal 'lcamtuf' Zalewski. The homepage says it was created to merge the best features developed for the AFL family that were never merged into AFL, which has not been updated since November 2017. The README calls it "a superior fork to Google's AFL - more speed, more and better mutations, more and better instrumentation, custom module support, etc."
entry.install:
brew install afl++
# The README's first suggested route is Docker instead: docker pull aflplusplus/aflplusplus
# You also need a target whose source you can rebuild with afl-cc, plus some seed input files.

Rebuilds a target project with AFL++'s compiler wrappers so it is instrumented.
Starts fuzzing a program that reads stdin, with the live status screen and results in output_dir.

entry.whats_unique: It merges years of AFL improvements that never made it upstream into one maintained project, with several instrumentation modes including binary-only ones. Its license is also unusual: a per-file split, plus a commercial option paid as a donation to a good cause.
entry.caveats: The dev branch is described as 'bleeding edge', and afl-fuzz is AGPL-3.0, so commercial use needs compliance or the EUR 20,000 donation license; the README also urges reading docs/fuzzing_in_depth.md before starting.
